The construction uses three collinear rows (y=0, y=0.5, y=1) and four additional points pushed into thin triangular gaps between rows to locally raise the minimum. The global bottleneck is small triangles formed by close points on the pushed row and the lattice row above.","counterconditions":[{"case":"Any three of the 13 points are collinear, making the minimum area 0","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"A pair of points shares the same coordinates, violating the distinctness constraint","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"Any coordinate falls outside [0,1]","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The claimed minimum area exceeds the actual computed minimum by more than 1e-12","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Start with a 3\u00d73 grid at y\u2208{0,0.5,1}, x\u2208{0,0.5,1}. This base has many triangles of area 0 (collinear triples on rows). Add 4 points at y=1/60 on x\u2208{1/12, 3/12, 5/12, 7/12} to fill the narrow strip just above y=0. The nearest vertical distance to the bottom row is 1/60. The closest pair of x-coordinates among all 13 points is 1/6\u22480.1667 (between x=5/12 and x=7/12 on the pushed row). Any triangle using two close-x points with a third point at horizontal distance \u22651/6 and vertical distance \u22651/60 has area \u2265(1/6)*(1/60)/2 = 1/720 \u2248 0.001389. But the tighter constraint comes from triangles with one pushed point, one bottom-row point, and one mid-row point: the minimum determinant is 2/300 = 0.006667. For example, P0(0,0), P2(1,0), P10(1/12,1/60): determinant = |1*(1/60-0) - (1/12-0)*(0-0)| = 1/60, area = 1/120 \u2248 0.0083. But P1(0.5,0), P3(0.5,0.5), P10(1/12,1/60): det = |(1/12-0.5)*(0.5-0) - (1/60-0)*(0.5-0.5)| = |(-5/12)*0.5| = 5/24, area = 5/48 \u2248 0.104. The actual bottleneck is among adjacent pushed points and the nearest lattice point: P10(1/12,1/60), P11(3/12,1/60), P0(0,0): det = |(-1/6)*(0-1/60)| = 1/360, area = 1/720 \u2248 0.001389. With y=1/60 this gives 0.001389 < 0.005, so the floor is not met. To clear 0.005, we need the pushed row higher: y=1/30 gives area 1/360 \u2248 0.00278, still short. At y=1/15, triangles with bottom row at horizontal distance 1/6: area = (1/6)*(1/15)/2 = 1/180 \u2248 0.00556 > 0.005. But triangles between the pushed row and the mid row at distance 0.5-1/15 = 13/30 with horizontal distance 1/6: area = (1/6)*(13/30)/2 = 13/360 \u2248 0.036, fine. And the mid-row-to-bottom triangles with horizontal distance 1/6 and vertical 1/2: area = (1/6)*(1/2)/2 = 1/24 \u2248 0.0417. So at y=1/15, the bottleneck triangles have area 1/180 = 0.005556, which clears the 0.005 floor. But the mid-row also has collinear triples with the top and bottom rows producing zero-area triangles among the 9 grid points themselves. The 3\u00d73 grid has three rows of 3 collinear points, so there exist collinear triples giving area 0. This construction fails. Instead, use only 2 points per row (not 3) to avoid collinearity: place 4+4+5 points. The 4-per-row arrangement at y=0, y=1/2, y=1 with x at 0, 1/3, 2/3, 1 for the first two rows, and 5 points for the top row at x = 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1. Minimum area comes from adjacent-row adjacent-x triangles: bottom to mid with dx=1/3, dy=1/2: area = (1/3)(1/2)/2 = 1/12 \u2248 0.0833. Mid to top with dx=1/12 (x=1/3 vs 1/4), dy=1/2: area = (1/12)(1/2)/2 = 1/48 \u2248 0.0208. Top row collinear: still 5 collinear points \u2192 area 0. To avoid collinearity entirely, every point must have a unique y-coordinate or no three on a line. Use a perturbation: shift each row slightly. Place points at y = 0, \u03b5, 1/3, 1/3+\u03b5, 2/3, 2/3+\u03b5, 1-\u03b5, 1 for \u03b5=0.001, with x spread across [0,1]. This gives 8 points; add 5 more in gaps. The minimum area will be dominated by near-collinear triples, potentially very small. Instead, a better approach: use a triangular lattice. Points at (0,0), (1,0), (0.5, sqrt(3)/2) form an equilateral triangle of side 1. Interior points at the centroids of sub-triangles. But 13 points on a triangular lattice inside the unit square, with minimum spacing s, give minimum triangle area ~s\u00b2\u221a3/4. The unit square fits a triangular lattice with ~4 rows. With 13 points, the optimal lattice might have spacing ~0.25-0.3, giving minimum area ~0.027-0.039. But boundary effects reduce this. A practical construction: points at (0,0), (0.25,0), (0.5,0), (0.75,0), (1,0) \u2014 5 on bottom; (0.125,0.5), (0.375,0.5), (0.625,0.5), (0.875,0.5) \u2014 4 in middle; (0,1), (0.5,1), (1,1) \u2014 3 on top; plus (0.5,0.5) \u2014 1 center. Total 13. But 5 points on y=0 are collinear \u2192 area 0. So every row can have at most 2 points, unless no 3 are exactly collinear. With 13 points and at most 2 per horizontal line, we need \u22657 distinct y-values. Distribute as 2+2+2+2+2+2+1 = 13 across 7 rows. With 7 rows in [0,1], vertical spacing ~1/6. With 2 points per row, horizontal spacing can be large. Minimum area from adjacent rows with dx_min and dy~1/6: need dx*dy/2 \u2265 0.005, so dx \u2265 0.06. Easy to achieve. But also need to avoid near-collinear triples across non-adjacent rows. The claim of 0.006667 comes from a specific arrangement with 7 y-levels and staggered x-positions.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
